newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Bank of Thailand caught in rate cut dilemma.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bank of Thailand caught in rate cut dilemma.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand is in a policy dilemma over cutting interest rates, torn between a government push for economic recovery and a need to defend the baht, economists and analysts said on Thursday.

Analysts concurred that the central bank would favour lower rates to boost the economy, but were not so sure whether it would make a more determined move to lower rates by cutting its discount rate soon.

Fears of a capital flight and the threat of attacks on the baht, which could remain as long as investors had doubts about Thai economic fundamentals, would force the central bank to take a cautious stance on rates despite finance ministry pressure for cuts, they said.
The discount rate, now at 10.50 percent, is the rate charged on loans by the central bank to commercial banks. The last time the central bank cut the discount rate was on March 1, 1995.
"I think the Bank of Thailand will announce the cut in the discount rate once they can come up with effective measures to deal with baht speculators," said an economist at a European investment bank.
There had been speculation in local media that a discount rate would take place last Wednesday but it did not materialise.
"There is no change in the discount rate yet. However, I'm not in a position to say if there will be one in the near future," central bank spokeswoman Daungmanee Vongprathip said.

"Generally, in determining whether the discount rate should be cut, several factors must be taken into account -- the currency stability and capital movement. As a developing country, Thailand still needs to import capital," she said.
Thailand keeps rates high to attract capital and to defend the baht against speculative attacks. The minimum lending rate at 12.75-13.00 percent is one of the highest in the region.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan has vigorously sought a 200 basis points cut in bank lending rates to stimulate an economy seen growing at its lowest rate in over a decade -- below official forecasts of six percent.

The central bank can influence commercial bank rates indirectly by injecting liquidity into the money market to keep the interbank rate low. But it could bring the rate down more directly by cutting the discount rate.

Olarn Chaiprawat, the Thai Bankers Association president, said on Wednesday that commercial banks would cut their lending rates by about 25 to 50 basis points after the central bank cut the discount rate.

But a heavy offshore speculative attack last week on the baht, which the central bank fought off effectively with support from regional central banks, would have an impact on any central bank decision on rates, analysts said.

"I don't see them delaying the decision very long. I would tend to think they would want to monitor the money market situation further to make sure...that their policy to cut supplies of baht to offshore players is effective enough," said Irene Tang, an economist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore.

But Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Singapore, said the Bank of Thailand was likely to be cautious in cutting the discount rate due to its need to defend the baht and capital inflows.

The Bank of Thailand successfully defended the baht last week from speculative attacks by imposing a ban on lending baht to offshore foreign buyers, but the measure could not last as the two-tier baht trading system it created was not in the spirit of a liberalised market, he said.

"In Thailand, no one solution will be able to address all the ills of the economy. (The authorities) need to sit down and come out with a consistent framework between fiscal and monetary policies," he said.
